transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-10-12 15:00 PDT · Duration 48m · Redwood: Maya, Ethan, Zara · Acme: Lena, Raj, Sophie

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we got most folks, cool. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, joining with Ethan and Zara from our SE squad. Quick agenda — walk through Optimize, batching, KV/prefix cache, then cost model examples, Q&A, and pilot next steps.

[00:17] Lena: Thanks Maya. We're really trying to understand where we can shave tokens and CPU, but keep 95/99 latency under 200 ms. We're running a mix of short chat and doc summarization flows.

[00:36] Ethan: Great. Quick clarifying question — do you have a single model family in prod or multiple sizes?

[00:42] Lena: Mostly a medium-sized open model, we also run a larger one for complex legal summarization. Throughput target about 120 QPS average, spiky to 400 at peak.

[01:05] Zara: Perfect, that profile is actually where we see big wins from both batching and prefix/KV caching. I'll start with batching basics, then Ethan will do a KV cache run-through and cost numbers.

[01:18] Zara: So continuous batching — instead of waiting for a fixed batch size we adaptively batch incoming requests for a short window (tens of ms) to improve GPU utilization. For your 120 QPS baseline that often means batch sizes of 8-32 depending on token length. There's a latency tradeoff but for summary flows where tokens are 200-500 it's usually net positive.

[01:45] Raj: Real quick, how do you prevent tail latency from ballooning when you wait to fill batches? We can't degrade 99th perc for payments flows.

[01:53] Ethan: Great question. We use hybrid policies — target latency windows plus priority routing. So high-priority paths bypass batching or use smaller micro-batches; normal traffic gets larger batches. Also warm KV cache reduces generation time because the KV cache avoids recomputing prefixes.

[02:18] Sophie: When you say KV cache you mean prefix caching of hidden states? We've seen docs call it KV cash in notes, haha.

[02:25] Ethan: (laughs) Yeah sometimes transcription calls it cash. It's KV cache — storing key/value cache for repeated prefixes so when you continue a conversation or re-run similar prompts you avoid repeated attention compute. Two modes: prefix cache (server-side prefix reuse) and per-request KV hits.

[02:47] Maya: I'll share on the chat a link to the cost model spreadsheet — it's a sample with your traffic profile plugged in.

[02:55] [link: redwood_cost_model_acme_sample.xlsx]

[03:01] Ethan: Walkthrough of the sheet — column A is request type (short chat, long summary), B is avg tokens out, C tokens in, D is QPS, then we model per-token GPU compute and amortized overhead. Key levers: batch size, cache hit rate, and sequence length.

[03:25] Ethan: Example 1: chat path with 20 token responses, no cache — cost X. If we enable prefix caching with a 65% hit rate and batching to avg batch 16, cost drops ~45-55% in that row. For long summary path, KV cache hit rates are lower; batching yields more of the gains there.

[03:50] Raj: Do you have recommended cache sizes / retention TTLs? We can't keep everything forever for PII reasons.

[03:57] Zara: TTLs are policy-driven. For most customers we suggest a 1-7 day rolling hot cache for high-frequency prefixes and strict TTLs for PII. We also support encryption at rest and KMS-managed keys.

[04:15] Sophie: Can we integrate with our HSM/KMS? Auditors will want to see key lifecycle.

[04:21] Maya: Yes — Redwood Private and Dedicated support KMS integrations and you can bring your own keys. We'll add the network diagrams and KMS notes to the packet.

[04:30] [05:00] Ethan: Diving into latency numbers — with batching the per-token throughput improves but per-request latency has a small median increase for tiny requests. For your 95/99 constraints, we recommend hybrid routing: critical payment decisions go through low-latency path (no batching or micro-batch of 2-4) while conversational or summaries use larger batches and KV caching.

[05:25] Lena: What about model variants? Could we use a smaller quantized model for first-pass intent and larger for final summary?

[05:32] Ethan: Absolutely. That's a common pattern — use cheap quantized smaller model or distilled variant for candidate generation, then fall back to a bigger model for high-confidence outputs. Redwood supports automated fallback policies.

[05:50] Raj: Curious about how batching works with streaming responses — many of our integrations use streaming to show partial replies.

[05:58] Zara: Streaming and batching are orthogonal. We stream tokens as the model produces them; batching traditionally just organizes the forward passes. For very low-latency streaming we recommend smaller micro-batches and prefix cache to reduce compute.

[06:20] [06:40] Ethan: Now cost model math quick: assume 1k tokens/sec baseline, GPU p100 (example) cost per hour Y; with batching and a 60% cache hit we can reduce GPU hours by ~40%. Remember that cache hit doesn't reduce token billing if you're using third-party billing, but it reduces compute and instance hours on Redwood Dedicated.

[06:58] Lena: Important distinction — we bill internal cost center on instance hours, so compute reduction matters more than token counts.

[07:05] Maya: Right — for Dedicated/private deployments the Optimize levers map to dollars saved on infra. For hosted API we still have per-token pricing but caching+batches lower your per-response latency and unit cost in practice.

[07:25] Raj: Any gotchas around cache consistency? If a user updates a doc, do we risk stale summaries?

[07:33] Ethan: You can invalidate cache keys on update events; we also expose TTLs and namespacing so you can segment per-customer or per-doc. Best practice: event-driven invalidation in your pipeline.

[07:50] Sophie: How much engineering effort to integrate? Our stack is Kubernetes + Envoy + internal auth.

[07:57] Zara: For Dedicated we provide a connector and Helm charts; for Private it's a packaged deploy. Most customers do an initial integration week and then pilot runs. We'll include the runbook in follow-ups.

[08:15] [08:32] Maya: Quick live demo — Ethan, can you show the spreadsheet scenario for Acme's chat traffic?

[08:33] Ethan: Sure — sharing screen now.

[08:40] [screen share: cost model]

[08:44] Ethan: Here we plug your QPS 120, token distribution from the sample logs you sent. Row 12 shows baseline cost, row 13 shows with batching to avg batch 18 and 50% KV hit — you can see GPU-hours drop and dollar-estimate drops about 38%. There's also sensitivity table for cache hit rate from 0 to 80%.

[09:10] Raj: That sensitivity table is super helpful. Do you have the raw formulas so we can run in-house?

[09:15] Ethan: Yep — we'll send the sheet with formulas and an export of the assumptions. That's part of the next steps.

[09:22] Lena: On security, can you log what changes happened to cached items? We need an audit trail for compliance.

[09:30] Maya: Yes, Redwood emits audit logs and access events; we can map those to your SIEM. We'll add sample logs to the packet.

[09:45] [10:10] Ethan: Another nuance — prefix cache helps a ton for chat where users reuse system prompts. For long documents, you may get partial reuse if people ask similar follow-ups. You should instrument to measure actual cache hit rates before committing to TTLs.

[10:30] Sophie: Sounds reasonable. How long do most customers run pilots? We want to make sure we see real savings before committing to Reserved capacity.

[10:38] Maya: Usually 2-4 weeks for a pilot with targeted workloads; one week to integrate, 1-3 weeks to collect stable metrics. Then we can model Reserved capacity if the economics justify it.

[10:55] Raj: Is there any integration with our existing vector DB? We use Pinecone for embeddings.

[11:02] Ethan: We don't have a direct Pinecone plugin for caching, but you can combine results — prefix/KV cache is internal to the serving runtime; embedding stores remain your choice. No conflict there.

[11:20] Lena: One more — we have strict data residency in EU for a subset of traffic. How granular is routing by region?

[11:27] Zara: You can route requests by policy so EU traffic stays in EU regions; we also support private deployments in your VPC for strict residency.

[11:40] [11:55] Maya: We're about halfway through — any burning questions before we move to pilot plan?

[12:00] Lena: Just confirm: pilot will validate cost savings for our two main flows and measure 95/99 latency.

[12:07] Ethan: Correct — we'll instrument both chat and long summary flows, measure cache hit, batch sizes, median/95/99 pcts, and GPU hours.

[12:18] Maya: I'll recap next steps in chat and drop the links.

[12:25] [chat posted: redwood_cost_model_acme_sample.xlsx, runbook_link, SOC2_packet_link]

[12:40] Sophie: Good. I'm going to get legal looped in once we see the SOC2 packet.

[12:47] Raj: I'll pull logs and get you a sample token distribution and request trace by tomorrow.

[12:55] Maya: Awesome. Last quick note on guardrails — we can set per-route limits, fallback to smaller models, and observe quality regressions via our evals tooling. We'll also show you how to set up alarms for regression.

[13:12] Lena: Thanks all. This was very helpful.

[13:18] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and schedule the pilot kickoff for next week.

[13:25] End of call.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors (KV cash), speaker overlaps, and shorthand. References to shared artifacts: redwood_cost_model_acme_sample.xlsx, runbook link, SOC2_packet_link.
